title: CSS Grid
summary: Grid is the two-dimensional layout model — rows and columns defined together so content aligns across both axes at once. Learn tracks, areas, the fr unit, and when it beats flexbox outright.

slides.markdown:
[Flexbox](flexbox) solved one-dimensional layout — a row or a column. Grid solves the harder problem: laying content out in **rows and columns at the same time**, where a cell in row 3 aligns to the same column boundaries as a cell in row 1, by construction rather than coincidence.

This is the layout model behind dashboards, photo galleries, and page skeletons — anywhere you'd sketch a layout on paper as a grid of boxes before writing a line of CSS. Before Grid existed, this required floats, table layout hacks, or a scaffolding of nested flex containers that broke the moment content lengths varied.

The mental shift Grid asks for: you define the **structure first** — how many tracks, how big — then place items into it, rather than letting content push and pull the layout the way flow and flexbox do.

slides.subTitle: Tracks, lines, areas, gaps
slides.markdown:
`display: grid` turns a container's children into grid items placed inside a structure you define explicitly:

- **Tracks** — the rows and columns themselves, sized with `grid-template-rows`/`grid-template-columns`.
- **Lines** — the numbered boundaries between and around tracks. Line 1 is before the first track; line -1 is after the last, counting from the end.
- **Areas** — one or more cells grouped and given a name, so you can place an item by name instead of by line number.
- **Gaps** — the space between tracks, set with `gap` (or `row-gap`/`column-gap` independently), never adding space at the outer edge.

The key difference from flexbox: you're not asking items to distribute themselves along a line. You're declaring the grid's shape up front, and every item slots into that pre-defined structure — which is exactly what lets rows and columns line up across the whole layout.

Three tools do almost all the track-sizing work in real layouts:

- **`fr`** — a fraction unit meaning "one share of whatever space is left" after fixed-size tracks are subtracted. `grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 1fr` gives a fixed 200px sidebar and two equal-width columns splitting the rest.
- **`repeat()`** — avoids writing the same track size N times. `repeat(4, 1fr)` is identical to `1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr`.
- **`minmax(min, max)`** — a track that never shrinks below `min` or grows past `max`. `minmax(200px, 1fr)` gives a column that grows to fill space but never gets uncomfortably narrow.

Combine them and you get the pattern behind almost every responsive card grid on the web: `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))` — as many 200px-minimum columns as fit the container, each stretching evenly to fill remaining space, with zero media queries.

slides.sectionTitle: A dashboard laid out with named areas
slides.markdown:
The `grid-template-areas` string from the previous slide maps directly onto a visual layout: a full-height sidebar on the left, and a header/content/footer stack on the right sharing the remaining column.

Because the sidebar's name appears in all three rows of the areas string, it automatically spans all three rows without any explicit `grid-row: 1 / 4` — the area definition itself encodes the span. That's the payoff of naming regions: the spanning behavior falls out of the ASCII-art shape rather than needing separate span declarations.

slides.subTitle: What happens when content overflows
slides.markdown:
The **explicit grid** is what you defined with `grid-template-columns`/`grid-template-rows`. The **implicit grid** is what the browser creates automatically when items overflow that definition — more children than cells, for instance.

By default, overflow items create new *rows*, sized by content (`auto`). Control that with `grid-auto-flow: column` to overflow into new columns instead, and control the *size* of those auto-generated tracks with `grid-auto-rows`/`grid-auto-columns` — for example `grid-auto-rows: 120px` keeps every overflow row a consistent height instead of shrink-wrapping to content.

The practical gotcha: if you forget to set `grid-auto-rows`, a grid that receives more items than you planned for (a paginated list that grows, say) will silently produce rows of wildly inconsistent height instead of erroring — worth checking explicitly when a grid's item count is dynamic.

slides.subTitle: One dimension vs two
slides.markdown:
| | Flexbox | Grid |
|---|---|---|
| Dimensions | one axis at a time | rows and columns together |
| Sizing driver | content, then space distributed by grow/shrink | structure defined up front, content placed into it |
| Multi-line alignment | lines don't coordinate with each other | rows/columns align across the whole grid |
| Best for | toolbars, nav bars, tag lists, form rows | page skeletons, dashboards, card/photo grids |

The test that decides it: if you can describe the layout as "a row of things" or "a column of things," even one that wraps, it's a flexbox problem. If you'd sketch it on paper as an actual grid — content that needs to line up in both directions — it's a Grid problem.

Most production pages use both: Grid for the page shell, flexbox for the components living inside each grid cell.

slides.sectionTitle: A responsive card grid with no media queries

slides.markdown:
Named areas are readable, but sometimes you need surgical placement — a hero image spanning the first two columns and two rows:

```css
.hero {
  grid-column: 1 / 3; /* from line 1 to line 3 = spans 2 columns */
  grid-row: 1 / 3;    /* spans 2 rows */
}
```

The `/` separates the start and end **lines**, not track counts — `1 / 3` spans two tracks because it covers the space between lines 1 and 3. The shorthand `grid-column: span 2` says "span two tracks from wherever auto-placement puts me" without naming explicit lines, useful when the item's exact position doesn't matter but its size does.

Mixing line-based placement with named areas in the same grid works fine — use whichever is clearer for a given item, rather than picking one style dogmatically for the whole layout.

slides.sectionTitle: Reaching for grid and flex in the same component
slides.markdown:
The pitfall isn't using Grid or Flexbox wrong individually — it's reaching for whichever one you learned first and forcing every layout through it. Two symptoms:

- **Building a two-dimensional layout in flexbox with nested rows of flex containers**, then fighting alignment drift when row heights vary — the exact problem Grid exists to solve, solved instead with a stack of workarounds (fixed heights, `align-items: stretch` everywhere) that break the moment content changes.
- **Building a one-dimensional toolbar in Grid** with `grid-template-columns: repeat(5, auto)`, when a plain flex row with `gap` does the same job with less code and doesn't require pre-declaring how many items there are.

A `1fr` fraction unit inside Grid and a `flex: 1` in flexbox solve visually similar problems for different reasons — the first divides *predefined tracks*, the second divides *leftover space along one axis*. Reaching for the wrong tool because the syntax looks similar is a common source of layouts that are technically correct but needlessly convoluted.

One long-standing Grid limitation: a nested grid inside a grid item is its own independent grid, so its rows/columns don't align to the parent's tracks — a card's internal image/title/price rows can't line up with the *sibling* card's rows unless every card happens to have identical content heights.

`grid-template-columns: subgrid` (and the row equivalent) fixes exactly this: a nested grid inherits its parent's tracks instead of defining its own, so a card grid where each card is itself a mini-grid can have its internal rows align perfectly across every card in the row. Support is solid in current evergreen browsers but worth a caniuse check if the project has a hard baseline requirement.

Mentioning subgrid unprompted in an interview signals you've hit the real-world case it fixes — nested component grids that need cross-alignment — rather than only knowing Grid at the tutorial level.

"Build me a dashboard layout with a fixed sidebar, a header, and a scrollable content area" is a common live-coding ask specifically because it tests whether you reach for Grid without hesitation.

A strong walkthrough names the pieces before writing code: "two columns — a fixed sidebar and a flexible content column; three rows — header, content, footer, with the sidebar spanning all three." Then the CSS is almost a transcription of that sentence, using `grid-template-columns`, `grid-template-rows`, and `grid-template-areas` together.

The follow-up an interviewer often adds — "now make the content area scroll independently while the sidebar stays fixed" — is solved with `overflow-y: auto` on the content area plus `height: 100vh` on the grid container, not with Grid properties at all. Recognizing when the next requirement is a Grid concern versus a plain overflow/height concern is part of what's being evaluated.
